Unit 4 • SL

Algorithmic Control

Introduction

How do programs make decisions and repeat tasks efficienty?

This unit moves from data storage to the mechanics of logic. You will explore how programs decide what to do next (Selection), how they repeat tasks (Iteration), and how we organise code into reusable modules. You will also learn to measure the efficiency of your solutions using Big O Notation.

You'll start with fundamental logic control (if/else, loops). Then, you'll apply this to master standard algorithms for sorting and searching data, analyzing which methods are faster. Finally, you'll learn to make your data persist by reading and writing to files.

Logic & Control Flow

Programs are not just linear lists of instructions. We control the flow using:

  • Selection: Making decisions (e.g., if password == "123": enter()).
  • Iteration: Repeating tasks (e.g., while user_is_active: keep_running()).
  • Sequencing: Ensuring instructions happen in the correct order.

Standard Algorithms

Computer Science has standard "recipes" for common problems. You will master:

  • Searching: Finding an item. Linear Search (check one by one) vs Binary Search (divide and conquer).
  • Sorting: Organizing data. Bubble Sort (swapping neighbors) vs Selection Sort (finding the minimum).

Efficiency (Big O)

Not all correct solutions are good solutions. We measure efficiency using Big O Notation to predict how an algorithm performs as data grows.

  • O(1): Constant time (instant).
  • O(n): Linear time (more data = more time).
  • O(n²): Quadratic time (slow! e.g., nested loops).

File Processing

Variables die when the program ends. To save data, we use Persistent Storage.

  • Read: Loading data from a file into memory.
  • Write: Overwriting a file with new data.
  • Append: Adding new data to the end of an existing file.

Key Terminology
TermDefinition
SelectionA programming construct where a section of code is run only if a condition is met (If/Else).
IterationRepeating a block of code a specific number of times (For) or until a condition changes (While).
Big O NotationA formal notation used to describe the performance or complexity of an algorithm.
Linear SearchChecking every element in a list one by one until the target is found.
Binary SearchAn efficient search that divides a sorted list in half repeatedly.
Bubble SortA simple sort that repeatedly steps through the list, swaps adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order.
Selection SortA sort that repeatedly finds the minimum element and moves it to the beginning.
Persistent StorageData storage that retains data after the power to the computer is turned off (e.g., Files).

Common Misconceptions

Binary Search on Unsorted Lists

Attempting to run Binary Search on a jumbled list. It won't work! The data MUST be sorted first.

Bubble Sort Efficiency

Believing Bubble Sort is 'good' because it's easy to code. It is actually very slow (O(n²)) for large datasets.

File Modes

Confusing 'w' (write - which deletes existing content) with 'a' (append - which adds to it).

  • Database query optimization
  • Save game files
  • Log files for servers

Think Deeper

"Is efficiency always the goal?" Is a highly efficient but complex algorithm better than a slightly slower but readable one? When might 'Good Enough' be better than 'Perfect'?
